cards.back: Make repeated passes through the list, comparing each adjacent pair and swapping any pair that is out of order, until a complete pass makes no swaps at all.

keyPoints.text: compare adjacent items
swap any pair that is out of order
repeat passes until no swaps occur
synonyms: the largest value bubbles to the end

cards.explanation: After the first pass the largest item is guaranteed to be in its final position, which is why each pass can ignore one more item at the end.

cards.back: Recursively split the list in half until every sublist holds a single item, then repeatedly merge pairs of sorted sublists back together in order until one sorted list remains.

keyPoints.text: split the list in half recursively
merge sorted sublists back together
continues until one sorted list remains

cards.explanation: Merging two already-sorted lists only needs one pass through each, which is why the cost per level is O(n) and there are log n levels.

cards.front: State the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort and of merge sort.
cards.back: Bubble sort is O(n^2) and merge sort is O(n log n).

keyPoints.text: bubble sort is O(n^2)
merge sort is O(n log n)

mcq.correct: Bubble sort is O(n^2) and merge sort is O(n log n).
distractors: Bubble sort O(n log n), merge sort O(n^2)

cards.explanation: Bubble sort's nested passes over n items give n^2 comparisons; merge sort's log n levels of O(n) work give n log n.

cards.front: Describe the insertion sort algorithm and say when it performs well.
cards.back: Take each item in turn and insert it into its correct position among the items already sorted before it, shifting them up to make room. It performs well on small lists and on lists that are already nearly sorted, where few shifts are needed.

keyPoints.text: insert each item into the sorted part before it
works well on small lists
works well on nearly sorted lists

cards.explanation: On already-sorted data insertion sort makes n comparisons and no shifts, so it runs in O(n) - better than merge sort in that special case.

cards.front: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?
cards.back: Equal keys keep their original relative order after sorting. Bubble, insertion and merge sort are stable when implemented in the usual way; a selection sort that swaps across several items is not.

keyPoints.text: equal items keep their original relative order
identifies a stable algorithm
identifies an unstable one

cards.explanation: Stability matters when sorting on a second key: sorting by name then by class keeps the names ordered within each class only if the sort is stable.

cards.front: How many comparisons does bubble sort make in the worst case on a list of 8 items, and how many passes is that?

keyPoints.text: 28 comparisons
7 passes

cards.explanation: On the first pass 7 comparisons are made, on the second 6, and so on down to 1, giving $7 + 6 + \ldots + 1 = 28$. This assumes the optimised version that does not re-examine the largest element already bubbled to the end. The answer 64 is $n^2$, which is the right order of growth but not the exact count - the distinction matters when a question asks how many.

cards.front: What is the space complexity of merge sort, and why does it need it?
cards.back: $O(n)$, because the two halves are merged into a separate array before being copied back.

keyPoints.text: O(n)
the merged result needs a separate array
it is not an in-place sort

cards.explanation: Merging two sorted halves into order cannot be done in place without extra storage, so merge sort needs an array the size of the input. The recursion stack adds only $O(\log n)$, which the $O(n)$ term dominates. This is the standard trade-off to quote: merge sort buys its guaranteed $O(n \log n)$ worst case with linear extra memory.

cards.front: Describe quick sort and state why its worst case is worse than merge sort's.
cards.back: A pivot is chosen, the list is partitioned into items below and above it, and each side is sorted recursively. The worst case is $O(n^2)$, which happens when the pivot is repeatedly the smallest or largest item, giving partitions of size $n - 1$ and 0.

keyPoints.text: choose a pivot and partition the list
synonyms: split into two sides of the pivot

keyPoints.text: sort each side recursively
worst case is O(n^2)
it happens when the pivot is always an extreme value
synonyms: already sorted list with first element as pivot

mcq.correct: $O(n^2)$ when the pivot is repeatedly an extreme, giving one empty partition
distractors: It has no worst case better than merge sort

cards.explanation: The classic trigger is taking the first element as the pivot on an already sorted list: each partition puts $n - 1$ items on one side and nothing on the other, so the recursion is $n$ deep and the work is $1 + 2 + \ldots + n$. Choosing the pivot at random, or using the median of three, makes this very unlikely, which is why quick sort is usually the faster choice in practice despite the worse bound.

cards.front: When does insertion sort run in $O(n)$ time, and why is that useful?
cards.back: When the list is already sorted or nearly so, because each item is compared with only the few before it and makes almost no swaps. It is why real sorting libraries switch to insertion sort for small or nearly sorted sections.

keyPoints.text: when the data is already sorted or nearly sorted
each item moves only a short distance
synonyms: few comparisons and swaps per item

keyPoints.text: libraries use it for small sections
synonyms: combined with merge or quick sort

mcq.correct: On sorted or nearly sorted data, because items barely move
distractors: On randomly ordered data of any size
When the list has fewer than 10 items, always

cards.explanation: In the best case each item is compared once with the item before it and swapped not at all, giving $n - 1$ comparisons. The number of swaps equals the number of inversions in the input, which is what makes insertion sort adaptive - its cost tracks how disordered the data actually is. Merge sort does not have this property and takes the same time on sorted data as on random data.

cards.front: Which of bubble sort, insertion sort, merge sort and quick sort are stable, and why does stability matter?
cards.back: Bubble, insertion and merge sort are stable; quick sort is not. Stability matters when sorting on more than one key, so that the order established by an earlier key is preserved.

keyPoints.text: bubble, insertion and merge sort are stable
synonyms: equal items keep their relative order

keyPoints.text: quick sort is not stable
synonyms: partitioning can swap equal items past each other

keyPoints.text: stability matters for multi-key sorting

mcq.correct: Bubble, insertion and merge stable; quick sort not
distractors: Bubble and quick stable; insertion and merge not

cards.explanation: Stability means two records judged equal keep the order they started in. Sorting a list of people by forename and then by surname with a stable sort leaves them ordered by surname and, within each surname, by forename - the reverse order of sorting works only if the sort is stable. Quicksort's long-distance swaps break this.

cards.front: You must sort a list of 30 items that is usually almost in order. Which sort would you choose, and why?
cards.back: Insertion sort. On nearly sorted data it runs close to $O(n)$, it needs no extra memory and its simplicity makes it easy to implement correctly for so small a list.

keyPoints.text: insertion sort
it is near linear on nearly sorted data
synonyms: almost in order is its best case

keyPoints.text: it is in place and simple
synonyms: easy to get right for a small list

mcq.correct: Insertion sort: near-linear on nearly sorted data, in place and simple
distractors: Quick sort: fastest in the average case

cards.explanation: The asymptotic advantage of $O(n \log n)$ does not pay off at $n = 30$, where the constant factors and the extra memory of merge sort cost more than they save. This is exactly the reasoning behind hybrid sorts, which use insertion sort below a threshold of a few dozen items. Choosing an algorithm is a decision about the data and the size, not only about the complexity class.

cards.front: Trace one pass of insertion sort on the list 7, 3, 5, 1, starting from the second item.
cards.back: Take 3: it is less than 7, so 7 moves up and 3 goes first, giving 3, 7, 5, 1. The sorted region now holds 3 and 7.

keyPoints.text: the item being inserted is 3
7 shifts one place to the right
the list becomes 3, 7, 5, 1

cards.explanation: Insertion sort keeps a sorted region on the left and grows it one item at a time by shifting larger items right until a gap opens. Completing it: 5 is inserted before 7 to give 3, 5, 7, 1, then 1 shifts all three up to give 1, 3, 5, 7. Notice that items shift rather than swap, which is what makes the best case $O(n)$.
